subject: Archaeology
title: The Ishtar Gate: Babylon's Blue Wonder
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Ishtar Gate: Babylon's Blue Wonder.

hook.text: Babylon's main gate was covered in brilliant blue glazed bricks decorated with golden dragons and bulls.

buildup.text: King Nebuchadnezzar II built the Ishtar Gate around 575 BCE as the grand entrance to his capital city.

discovery.text: Robert Koldewey excavated it between 1902 and 1914. He shipped thousands of glazed bricks back to Berlin.

twist.text: The reconstructed gate now stands in Berlin's Pergamon Museum — the largest artifact in any museum. Iraq wants it back.

climax.text: The processional road leading to the gate was lined with 120 glazed lions — each one unique and six feet long.

punchline.text: Babylon's front door stands in Berlin. A hundred and twenty lions still guard the path.

quiz.question: Where is the reconstructed Ishtar Gate now located?
options: The Iraqi National Museum in Baghdad

details.summary: The Ishtar Gate was Babylon's grand entrance, covered in brilliant blue glazed bricks decorated with golden dragons and bulls. Built by Nebuchadnezzar II around 575 BCE, it was excavated by Robert Koldewey and reconstructed in Berlin's Pergamon Museum.
details.whyItMatters: The Ishtar Gate demonstrates Mesopotamian mastery of glazed brick technology and monumental architecture. Its reconstruction in Berlin raises questions about who owns ancient heritage and where it should be displayed.
takeaways: The Ishtar Gate featured blue glazed bricks with golden animals
Nebuchadnezzar II built it around 575 BCE at Babylon's entrance
Its Berlin reconstruction raises cultural heritage debates

faq.question: Why is the Ishtar Gate in Berlin instead of Iraq?
faq.answer: Robert Koldewey excavated it between 1902 and 1914 under Ottoman permission and shipped the bricks to Germany. Iraq has requested its return, but Germany retains it. The gate exemplifies the global debate over colonial-era acquisition of archaeological heritage.

faq.question: What animals decorate the Ishtar Gate?
faq.answer: Alternating rows of golden bulls (symbols of the storm god Adad) and dragons called mushussu (symbols of the city god Marduk). The animals were molded in relief from glazed brick against a deep blue background made from ground lapis lazuli.
